turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must have a reference for Lady Bloxham. I suppose you have one, Mr. Worthing?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I don't have any references from Lady Bloxham, but I'm sure she would be delighted to vouch for me if you were to ask her.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I'm afraid that is not sufficient, Mr. Worthing. I require a written reference from Lady Bloxham, not a promise of her good opinion.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I don't have any written references from Lady Bloxham, but I could try to fetch her from her home if it would be satisfactory to you, ma'am.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, your response is most unsatisfactory. I will not have you prancing about, fetching Lady Bloxham from her home, only to have her confirm the worst about your character.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I won't have you interrogating Jack like this, Mother. He's perfectly suitable as a husband for me, and I won't have you questioning his character.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I assure you, Lady Bracknell, that my character is sound, and I hope that Gwendolen's opinion, which I know you value, will be taken into account.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, your audacity is quite remarkable, but it will not save you from my scrutiny.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I humbly apologize if my previous responses have caused any offense, Lady Bracknell. I assure you that my intention is only to prove myself worthy of Gwendolen's hand.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must insist on hearing the details of your family history, Mr. Worthing, as it is imperative that I understand the background of the man who wishes to marry my daughter.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I come from a respectable family, Lady Bracknell, although I must admit that my uncle's name is not actually Worthing, but Ernest Brougham. My mother, as you may know, was a Wardle, and I've always tried to live up to the standards of the Worthing name.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I am not impressed by your attempts to gloss over the irregularities in your family history, Mr. Worthing. A mere change of name does not magically erase the stain of illegitimacy.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I understand your concerns, Lady Bracknell, and I assure you that I have done everything in my power to rectify the situation, despite the circumstances of my birth.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must inform you, Mr. Worthing, that your assertions of rectifying the situation only raise more questions.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I must admit, Lady Bracknell, that the circumstances of my birth are not ideal, but I hope you can see that I have done my best to make a respectable life for myself, despite the mistakes of my father.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Your father, I believe, was a solicitor, was he not? And a man of some repute, I am told.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I-I'm afraid there's a bit of a misunderstanding, Lady Bracknell. My father was, in fact, a solicitor, but I'm not sure that's entirely relevant to the matter at hand.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: And what, might I ask, is the nature of this 'misunderstanding' that you speak of, Mr. Worthing?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'd rather not speak ill of my father, Lady Bracknell, but if you insist on knowing, he was a bit of a...gentleman of leisure, I suppose, though not in the way that would be, ah, respectable.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, I am not impressed by your attempt to gloss over the fact that your father was a man of questionable character. As a mother, I have a certain...expectation for the sort of son-in-law I wish to welcome into our family.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, should his health permit him, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Yes, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: That is satisfactory. What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I don’t depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
